chunks: "I think of it as silicon versus physics.
Everything that is control and logic goes on the die: the voltage reference, error amplifier, oscillator, PWM comparator, soft start, current limit, thermal shutdown, UVLO and the gate drivers.
For low to mid current parts the two power FETs are integrated too, so the sync buck is one chip. What stays outside is anything that stores real energy or needs tolerance.
That is the inductor, the input and output capacitors, and the bootstrap capacitor between BST and the switch node.
Adjustable parts also have an external feedback divider, so I pick the output voltage with two resistors.

Depending on the part, the compensation network is either inside, or I get a COMP pin and have to build a Type II or Type III network myself, and I might have a resistor on a pin to set frequency or a cap to set soft-start time.
Then the trade-off is current. Integrated FETs make for a tiny solution but the die is also the heat source, so thermal limits cap the current.
Past that I'd move to a controller with external FETs, where I own the gate drive, dead time and layout."
